blocks.content: CPU is measured in a specific unit, millicores, and it behaves as what is called a "compressible" resource, a container using too much CPU gets slowed down, never killed for it.

CPU requests are expressed in millicores, a thousandth of a single CPU core, 500m means half a core, 1000m (or simply 1) means a full core, this fine-grained unit lets you request fractional CPU precisely.

blocks.alt: A precise, fractional unit for expressing CPU need

blocks.content:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m   # half of one CPU core

code.content:

  requests:
    cpu: 500m   # half of one CPU core

blocks.content: 2. How the Scheduler Uses These Values
blocks.text: 2. How the Scheduler Uses These Values

blocks.content: Exactly as covered in the general Resource Requests topic, the scheduler sums up the CPU requests of every Pod already on a node, and only places a new Pod there if enough CPU capacity genuinely remains unclaimed.

blocks.alt: Summed across every Pod on a node, to decide if a new one still fits

blocks.content: This is the important, defining characteristic of CPU as a resource: it is compressible, a process can simply be given less CPU time and slowed down, it is never fatal to exceed a CPU limit, the process just runs more slowly, covered directly in the Resource Limits topic's throttling behavior.

blocks.alt: Slowed down when scarce, never killed for needing more than it was allotted

blocks.content: A typical, modest service might request 250m, a quarter of a CPU core, as its baseline, real production values are usually derived from actually observing an application's typical CPU usage, not guessed at arbitrarily.

blocks.alt: A real, commonly seen value for a modest, everyday service

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: CPU is requested in millicores (500m = half a core), and the scheduler sums these values across a node to decide if a new Pod still fits.
CPU is a compressible resource, exceeding its limit results in throttling, not termination, a real, meaningful contrast with memory, covered next.
